subject: english
topic: Grammatical names and functions of words, phrases and clauses

kept.q: Identify the grammatical name of the underlined clause: 'Because the market women arrived late, the customers had already left.' (The underlined clause is 'Because the market women arrived late'.)
options: Main clause
Noun clause
Adverbial clause of reason
Relative clause
kept.explanation: The clause begins with 'Because' and explains why the customers had left, giving a reason. Clauses introduced by 'because' that explain cause are adverbial clauses of reason.
kept.pidgin: Di clause 'Because the market women arrived late' dey show us di reason why di customers leave. Na proper adverbial clause of reason be dat.

kept.q: In the sentence 'What Ngozi said at the meeting surprised everyone,' what is the function of the clause 'What Ngozi said at the meeting'?
options: It is an adjectival clause qualifying 'everyone'
It is an adverbial clause of manner
It is a noun clause functioning as the subject
It is an independent clause joined by coordination
kept.explanation: The clause 'What Ngozi said at the meeting' acts as the subject of the verb 'surprised', doing the job a noun would do. Clauses that act as subject, object or complement are noun clauses.
kept.pidgin: Dis clause 'What Ngozi said at the meeting' dey stand as di person wey do di work of subject for di sentence. Na correct noun clause be dat.

kept.q: Select the sentence in which 'running' functions as a gerund.
options: The running water flooded the compound
Running every morning keeps Tunde fit
He saw a running tap in the kitchen
The boys were running round the field
kept.explanation: In this option, 'Running' acts as the subject of the sentence, so it behaves like a noun. A gerund is a verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun.
kept.pidgin: Na only for option B 'Running' dey play di role of noun as subject of di sentence. Dat one na true gerund.

kept.q: In the sentence 'The man whose car was stolen reported to the police,' what is the grammatical name of 'whose car was stolen'?
options: Noun clause
Adjectival (relative) clause
Adverbial clause of condition
Main clause
kept.explanation: The clause 'whose car was stolen' gives more information about 'the man', describing him like an adjective would. Clauses beginning with relative pronouns such as 'whose' that qualify a noun are adjectival clauses.
kept.pidgin: Di clause 'whose car was stolen' dey explain more about di man, just like adjective dey do. Na adjectival or relative clause be dat.

kept.q: Read the sentence carefully: 'Having finished her assignment, Blessing decided to visit her aunt in Enugu before it got dark.' What is the grammatical function of 'Having finished her assignment'?
options: It is a noun phrase functioning as object
It is a non-finite (participial) phrase functioning adverbially
It is a finite adverbial clause of time
It is a main clause joined by a conjunction
kept.explanation: The phrase has no subject of its own and uses a participle 'Having finished', so it is non-finite, not a full clause. It shows the time relationship to the main action, functioning adverbially, like a reduced adverbial clause of time.
kept.pidgin: Dis phrase 'Having finished her assignment' no get subject and e start with participle, so e be non-finite phrase wey dey do adverb work. E correct well well.

q.q: Choose the option that correctly identifies the word class of the capitalised word: Chidinma spoke CONFIDENTLY during the debate competition.
options: Adjective
Adverb
Noun
Preposition
q.explanation: CONFIDENTLY describes how Chidinma spoke, telling us the manner of the action. Words ending in -ly that modify verbs are usually adverbs.

q.q: Which of the following sentences contains a word used as a conjunction?
options: Emeka ran FAST to catch the bus
The food was SO delicious that we asked for more
Please sit DOWN quietly
She bought a BEAUTIFUL necklace
q.explanation: In this sentence, 'so...that' links the clause to a result clause, making 'that' function as a subordinating conjunction introducing the result. The word joins two clauses together, which is the role of a conjunction.

rejected.why: ambiguous:‘That’ is a conjunction, but the capitalised ‘SO’ is an adverb; the intended word is unclear.|

q.q: In the sentence: 'The farmers in Benue State harvested a bountiful crop of yams,' what is the grammatical function of the underlined phrase 'in Benue State'? (Treat 'in Benue State' as the phrase under consideration.)
options: It functions as an adjectival phrase modifying 'farmers'
It functions as an adverbial phrase of place modifying 'harvested'
It functions as a noun phrase acting as subject
It functions as a prepositional phrase acting as object
q.explanation: The phrase 'in Benue State' describes which farmers, so it modifies the noun 'farmers' like an adjective. It answers the question 'which farmers?' not 'how or where harvested'.

rejected.why: review:The keyed option A is incorrect. 'in Benue State' modifies the verb 'harvested' telling us where they harvested, making it an adverbial phrase of place (Option B). The explanation also incorrectly claims it modifies 'farmers'.
